power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objectives: To examine which measure of socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions has the strongest relationship with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) among midlife and older lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, and other sexual and gender minority (LGBTQIA+) adults.
Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 3869 LGBTQIA+ adults aged 50 years or older participating in a community-engaged survey in California.
Using logistic regression, we examined overall associations between each indicator of socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions and SCD.
We used a dominance analysis to assess the relative importance of each indicator based on the proportion of variance in SCD it explained.
Results: Overall, 14.7% of the sample reported SCD.

Midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults in a lower socioeconomic position (i.e., lower education, unemployment, lower household income, fewer assets, financial insecurity, food insecurity, and unstable housing) had higher odds of SCD than those in a higher position, with significant odds ratios (OR) ranging from 1.28 to 2.55.
In contrast, perceiving one's community as safe for LGBTQIA+ people was associated with lower odds of SCD (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.38, 0.58).

Dominance analysis indicated that household assets was the most important factor, explaining 4.4% of the variance in SCD (95% CI 3.5%, 5.4%), followed by household income (2.9%; 95% CI 2.2%, 3.8%) and perceived community safety (2.2%; 95% CI 1.4%, 3.1%).
Discussion: Supporting the cognitive health of LGBTQIA+ people may require attention to both financial security across the life course and the broader social environments.

text.text: These conditions may become increasingly consequential for LGBTQIA+ people as they age and underscore the need to better address the social and economic needs that support healthy cognitive aging in this population.

In this study, we aimed to characterize the prevalence of SCD and its relationship to respondents' socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions in a community-based sample of midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults in California.

We focused on California given its rapidly growing population of both older adults and LGBTQIA+ people (Johnson, 2024; Johnson et al., 2025), and because addressing economic insecurity is a key priority among these groups (University of California, San Francisco, 2024).

text.text: We then aim to quantify the relative contribution of each social and economic factor that shaped SCD among midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults to understand which factors may be among the most important in relation to SCD.

This study is a secondary analysis of data collected through an online cross-sectional survey conducted from January to March 2024 to assess the health, well-being, and service needs of midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults living in California (University of California, San Francisco, 2024).
Participants were recruited using convenience sampling through a variety of outreach strategies led by Openhouse, a nonprofit organization that supports older LGBTQIA+ people.

These strategies included the creation of a statewide coalition of LGBTQIA+ service providers, distribution of flyers in community spaces, social media posts, newsletters, a dedicated website hosted by the California Department of Aging, and word-of-mouth among community members, senior service organizations, and events.
Additional details regarding community outreach are described elsewhere (University of California, San Francisco, 2024).

The eligibility criteria for the study were self-identifying as LGBTQIA+, being 50 years of age or older, and residing in California including community-dwelling older adults and those in senior living facilities.
The survey was administered online through Qualtrics (Qualtrics LLC, Provo, UT) and was available in Chinese, English, Spanish, and Tagalog, the most widely spoken languages in California.
Eligible participants were asked to provide informed consent for themselves, and those who completed the survey could choose to enter a drawing to win a $25 gift card.
The study was approved by the [redacted] Institutional Review Board.
Several steps were taken to ensure the quality of survey responses during data collection.
These included fraud and bot detection tools embedded in Qualtrics and manual reviews of potentially invalid responses.
Those identified as likely fraudulent or bot-generated (n = 406) or flagged as invalid during manual review (n = 2) were excluded from the dataset.
In addition, we excluded 168 participants with missing outcome data for the current analysis.

Subjective cognitive decline was assessed with a single self-reported question based on the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System Cognitive Decline module, "During the past 12 months, have you experienced confusion or memory loss that is happening more often or is getting worse?"
Response options included "yes", "no", and "I don't know/I'm not sure".
Those who responded affirmatively were considered to have experienced SCD.
We included nine indicators that captured participants' socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental condition.
1) Education level was categorized into four groups: high school diploma/GED or less, some college, 4-year college degree, and graduate degree.
2) Unemployment was dichotomized as a binary measure.

Participants were classified as unemployed if they did not report any form of employment (employed, working 1-39 hours per week; employed, working 40 or more hours per week; self-employed; or temporarily employed) and were not retired.
All others were considered unemployed.

3) Household income was categorized into five groups ranging from $30,000 or less to more than $120,000.4) Household assets were assessed by asking participants to estimate the total value of all assets owned by their household.

Responses were grouped into four categories from less than $10,000 to more than $500,000.5) Financial insecurity was assessed by asking whether participants had struggled to pay bills due to insufficient income in the past 12 months (yes or no).
6) Food insecurity was measured by asking how often participants worried about having enough money for nutritious meals in the past 12 months (yes or no).

7) Housing stability was assessed based on participants' current housing situation and categorized as stable if they reported having a steady place to live and unstable if they reported being worried about losing housing in the future or not having a steady place to live (e.g., in a shelter, living outside on the street).
8) Transportation was assessed by asking participants to select the methods they typically use to get where they need to go.
Participants who selected public transportation were categorized as relying on it; all others were categorized as not relying on public transportation.

9) LGBTQIA+ community safety was assessed through two questions asking how safe participants perceived their current community to be for 1) transgender, genderqueer, and non-binary individuals (gender minority safety) and 2) lesbian, gay, asexual, bisexual, and queer individuals (sexual minority safety), using a 5-point scale (1=extremely safe to5=extremely unsafe).

We then combined these responses to create a composite measure with four categories: safe for both gender and sexual minority people, safe for gender minority people only, safe for sexual minority people only, and unsafe for both groups.
Participants self-reported their ethnoracial identity, current gender identity, current sexual orientation, intersex status, place of birth, prior military service, and health insurance.
Participants could select multiple options for their ethnoracial identity, gender, and sexual orientation.
Sexual orientations were combined to create non-mutually exclusive groups: asexual, bisexual, gay/lesbian, queer, straight, and another sexual orientation.

Gender identities were cross stratified with sex assigned at birth to create mutually exclusive groups: cisgender men, cisgender women, gender diverse individuals assigned female at birth, gender diverse individuals assigned male at birth, transgender men, and transgender women.
Urban residence (yes or no) was based on self-reported ZIP code.
Age groups (50-59, 60-69, ≥70 years) was based on self-reported birthdate and categorized prior to data release to support deidentification.
HIV status was dichotomized as living with HIV for those reported "positive" and not living with HIV if otherwise.

Differences were assessed using t-test for continuous variables and chi-square or Fisher's Exact test for categorical variables.
Correlations were calculated between each socioeconomic and socioenvironmental indicator.

To evaluate associations between socioeconomic and socioenvironmental conditions and SCD, we fitted separate logistic regression models to estimate the unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (OR) and associated 95% confidence intervals (CI).

text.text: To calculate the relative importance of each socioeconomic and socioenvironmental condition on SCD in LGBTQIA+ midlife and older adults, we used an extension of the dominance analysis procedure that allows for the use of logistic regression (Azen & Traxel, 2009).

text.text: This approach assesses the change in variance for all possible subset models, allowing assessment of the relative importance of each predictor both alone and in the presence of all other combinations of predictors -that is, how much variance in the observed outcome can be attributed to one factor versus another.
However, unlike linear models that use the traditional R² , we used pseudo-R² measures, specifically McFadden's R² , to determine relative importance.

We opted for McFadden's R² due to its desirable statistical properties (Azen & Traxel, 2009), including boundness (values vary between 0 to 1), linear invariance (remains unchanged to linear transformation), monotonicity (value does not decrease when variables are added to the model), and intuitive interpretability.

text.text: We first fit a multivariable logistic model that included all socioeconomic and socioenvironmental factors while controlling for potential confounders as outlined in our main analysis, representing the total variance explained by our model.
Because the dominance analysis software does not support multiply imputed data, we used complete cases for this analysis.
We also refitted the same model with imputed data to assess the robustness of the results to the assumed missing data mechanism.

We then used the dominanceanalysis R package to decompose the total variance and evaluate the relative importance of each socioeconomic and environmental factors while keeping potential confounders constant across all models (Navarrete & Soares, 2025).

text.text: A bootstrap procedure with 1000 resamples was used to obtain general dominance values (i.e., proportion of variance explained for a given variable averaged across all model sizes) and the corresponding 95% percentile CI.

We report general dominance for our analysis to identify which socioeconomic and environmental factors that, on average, contribute most to explaining the variance in SCD among LGBTIQIA+ midlife and older adults.

We also reran the dominance analysis to determine whether the relative importance of each socioeconomic and socioenvironmental condition would change after accounting for mental health symptoms and substance use.
All analysis were conducted in R version 4.5.1.

text.text: In models that regressed SCD on education, household income, household assets, being in a lower position for any of these socioeconomic factors was associated with higher odds of SCD, with progressively stronger associations at lower socioeconomic positions.

For example, in adjusted models, respondents with the lowest household income and assets had 2.03 (95% CI 1.25, 3.31) times and 2.55 (95% CI 1.96, 3.32) times higher odds of SCD compared to the highest income and asset groups.

At moderate household income ($30,000-$60,000) and assets ($10,000-$100,000), respondents had 1.76 (95% CI 1.34, 2.31) times and 2.02 (95% CI 1.56, 2.62) times higher odds of SCD compared to the highest income and asset groups.

Similarly, unemployment, financial insecurity, food insecurity, unstable housing, reliance on public transportation were all associated with higher odds of SCD, with adjusted ORs ranging from 1.28 to 2.30.

Regarding LGBTQIA+ community safety, those who reported their community as safe for both sexual and gender minorities had lower odds of SCD (adjusted OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.38, 0.58) compared to those who felt their community was not safe.

Consistent with prior studies among midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults from population-based samples (Cicero et al., 2023; Flatt et al., 2021; Fredriksen-Goldsen et al., 2022; Hsieh et al., 2021), nearly 15% of midlife and older LGBTQIA+ respondents in this California sample reported SCD with higher percentages reported in certain subgroups such as bisexual and pansexual people as well as gender diverse people assigned male at birth.

text.text: Midlife and older LGBTQIA+ respondents with SCD were more likely to experience social and economic disadvantage compared to those without SCD, even after accounting for age, gender, ethnoracial groups, US birth, urban residence, prior military service, and HIV status.

The most important socioeconomic and socioenvironmental contributors to SCD were household assets (explaining 4.4% of the variance), followed by household income (2.9% of the variance) and community safety for LGBTQIA+ people (2.2% of the variance).

Other factors, such as unemployment, financial insecurity, housing instability, food insecurity, and education level, were found to be less important, with each factor explaining less than 1% of the variance in SCD.

Because our sample was predominantly cisgender and gay or lesbian, and include relatively more socially and economically advantaged respondents, these aggregate estimates may primarily reflect the experiences of these groups and mask subgroup differences in association of economic and social conditions with SCD for transgender and diverse people, bisexual people, and racially minoritized LGBTQIA+ people.
Thus, the observed associations may underestimate the potential magnitude of social and economic disparities in SCD among midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults.

Our result is consistent with the broader literature on social factors and SCD among the general population (Singh-Manoux et al., 2005; Lövdén et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025) and on research focusing on the economic marginalization LGBTQIA+ individuals experience and the proposed biological pathways between minority stress and physical health (Correro II & Nielson, 2020; Flentje et al., 2020 Flentje et al., , 2022;; Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Kinitz et al., 2025; Meyer, 2003).

text.text: Notably, in our study, associations between lower socioeconomic position and SCD remained robust after adjusting for mental health symptoms and substance use, though we observed attenuation of the explained SCD variance after accounting for mental health and substance use in the dominance analysis.

This suggests the potential importance of these factors for SCD in LGBTQIA+ individuals and highlight the need for future longitudinal research to better understand the mechanism between economic marginalization, mental health and substance use, and later-life cognitive decline.
An important contribution of our study is the identification of community safety as a socioenvironmental correlate of cognitive health in LGBTQIA+ populations.
Respondents who perceived their community as safe for sexual and/or gender minority individuals had 53% lower odds of reporting SCD.

Although research directly examining the association of community safety and SCD among LGBTQIA+ is limited, this result aligns with evidence examining the association of perceived community safety and physical health (Flentje et al., 2022).

text.text: These findings underscore the broader influence of the social environment on cognitive health in LGBTQIA+ populations and highlight the need for further research into the mechanisms through which community safety may shape SCD.

Results from dominance analysis further suggest that both financial security across the life course and the broader social environments may be the most relevant socioeconomic and socioenvironmental condition to SCD.
Household assets, which represent accumulated wealth over the life course (Krieger et al., 1997), were shown to explain the most variance in SCD.

text.text: One's assets (or lack thereof) may reflect the long-term consequences of earlier financial strains that leave LGBTQIA+ people unable to build their savings or possess the necessary financial resources to support cognitive aging and care in later life.

This is consistent with work suggesting that LGBTQIA+ individuals experience heightened employment precarity and economic marginalization related to minority stress (Kinitz et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2024), which may accumulate over time to shape cognitive health.

text.text: Because assets reflect long-term financial trajectories, they may be difficult to modify later in life, particularly for economically marginalized groups.

This highlights the potential value of future research focusing on interventions that promote financial security earlier in the life course, such as stable income opportunities and retirement and financial planning programs tailored to the needs of LGBTQIA+ communities.

By contrast, household income and perceived community safety highlight the potential relevance of policies and programs that address the current social and economic circumstances for midlife and older LGBTQIA+ people, especially those with SCD.

Such efforts may include addressing economic marginalization that LGBTQIA+ people face, such as unemployment, poorer job quality, and gender-based discrimination (Fredriksen Goldsen et al., 2022; Kinitz et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2024), which may contribute to fewer financial resources that would allow LGBTQIA+ people to live in communities with more supportive resources.

text.text: This study has several limitations.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretation, as cognitive impairment in older age may itself contribute to greater financial insecurity and poorer living conditions.
Second, the outcome was self-reported.

Prior work has noted that SCD is an imperfect indicator of objective cognitive impairment (Romanelli et al., 2024), and future studies would benefit from incorporating cognitive testing to better understand how socioeconomic and socioenvironmental conditions relate to cognitive decline.

text.text: Relatedly, the cross-sectional design does not allow us to examine changes in cognition over time, which may be more biologically relevant for understanding the influence of social and economic factors.
Third, selection bias is possible if LGBTQIA+ individuals experiencing greater economic marginalization and SCD were less likely to participate.
Fourth, our analyses assume no model misspecification and that included covariates were sufficient to control for confounding, though unmeasured confounding may be present.

Fifth, while minimal differences were observed between the multiple imputation and complete-case analysis, these methods may still be biased under missing-not-at-random or misspecification of the imputation model.

Sixth, participants included in this study were derived from a convenience, with an overrepresentation of White, cisgender, and gay/lesbian respondents and may not be representative of LGBTQIA+ individuals in California.
Furthermore, while the survey was offered in four languages, nearly all participants completed it in English.
These factors limit the generalizability of our findings.

Finally, our analyses considered LGBTQIA+ adults as an aggregate population and were not designed to examine heterogeneity in these associations across sexual orientation, gender identity, or intersecting social identities.

Prior research suggests that experiences of SCD may differ across sexual and gender minority subgroups and at the intersections of gender and ethnoracial identity (Cicero et al., 2023; Flatt et al., 2021).
